Sound technical approach: activation filtering to maintain sparsity across all backpropagation layers is mathematically well-justified with thorough backward graph analysis
Practical system design: clever handling of dynamic computation graphs through runtime stability assumption and special marker technique for dimension identification

weaknesses: Significant unresolved utility-efficiency trade-off: Collider achieves only 20.7% average accuracy compared to Rho's 24.8% (4.1 point regression), yet authors acknowledge this requires different hyperparameters without providing any empirical validation that the gap can be recovered

Very limited experimental scale: only tiny models (1.1B-1.5B) evaluated on single-node 8-GPU setup with no distributed training; unclear if 22% speedup generalizes to larger models (7B+) where results are more practically relevant

Limited baselines and comparisons: only compared against Rho filtering and standard training; no comparisons with other efficiency techniques or evaluation of interactions with other optimization methods like gradient checkpointing

strengths: Clear problem identification and motivation: The paper effectively demonstrates why existing token filtering achieves only 1.2% speedup despite filtering 40% of tokens, with well-illustrated analysis of gradient density propagation (Figures 3-4).

Technically sound core insight: Filtering activations to maintain sparsity across layers is well-reasoned, with proper mathematical analysis of backward computation in attention and FFN blocks (Equations 4-5).

Pragmatic implementation design: The automatic workflow using special markers to handle PyTorch's dynamic computation graphs (Section 3.2.3) is creative and practical; skeleton code generation via Torchgen is well-motivated.
Easy integration: Requires only one line of code for systems already using token filtering, with thoughtful offline/online separation (Figure 10).

Comprehensive evaluation scope for tested models: Testing across three models, nine tasks, context lengths (1K-4K), and filtering ratios (20%-70%) provides reasonable breadth, with clear figures (2, 3, 5, 7) effectively communicating the problem and solution.
weaknesses: Severe model scale limitation: Only 1.1B-1.5B parameter models evaluated, far below production LLMs (7B-70B+). Modern LLM architectures, memory/computation trade-offs, and dynamic graph complexity differ substantially at scale. Results on tiny models do not transfer to production systems, making this a critical limitation for an LLM-focused venue.

Contradicts main claims on utility: Collider achieves 20.7% average utility versus Rho's 24.8% (4.1% absolute decrease), contradicting the abstract's claim that 'Collider sustains the utility advancements of token filtering.' Section 6.2's dismissal as merely requiring 'different parameter settings' is unsupported—no systematic hyperparameter tuning is performed, suggesting Collider may be intrinsically different in learning dynamics.

Reference model overhead not addressed in practice: Assumes reference model is 'already trained' with offline inference results (Section 5.2), unrealistic in practice. While Section 4.3 discusses solutions (model compression, n-gram models), these are NOT implemented or evaluated. N-gram experiments (Figure 9) only show correlation without deployment results. Practitioners face full reference model cost, negating claimed efficiency gains.

Modest real-world speedup with high implementation complexity: End-to-end speedup of only 15-22% when filtering 40% is near theoretical maximum (40% × 66% backprop fraction ≈ 26%), but requires offline code generation, Torchgen, special markers, and operator overhead (0.87-1.14s per iteration, ~3% of total). ROI questionable for production deployments.

Incomplete experimental evaluation: (1) Only 1 epoch of training for utility evaluation—does not show long-term convergence or training dynamics; (2) No ablation studies to isolate contribution of activation filtering versus dimension reduction; (3) No hyperparameter tuning comparison—unfair to compare Rho and Collider with identical hyperparameters despite different gradient flows; (4) Limited to mathematical reasoning domain—generalization unclear; (5) No comparison with other efficiency techniques.

Activation filtering implications inadequately explored: Filtering softmax activations fundamentally changes gradient flow (acknowledged in Section 4.1), but the paper does not analyze what information is lost, how this affects convergence across multiple epochs, or whether the utility drop is inherent or just a hyperparameter mismatch. Section 4.1's discussion is insufficient for such a fundamental change to the learning process.

Limited scope of token filtering approach: Only evaluates one specific backward filtering method (Rho[20]) on one domain (mathematical reasoning). Unclear if benefits transfer to other token filtering strategies or task domains. Claim of 'unleashing full efficiency of token filtering' applies narrowly to one method.

Unvalidated distributed training claims: Section 4.2 claims benefits for tensor/sequence/pipeline parallelism but provides NO experimental validation. Communication savings are purely theoretical—critical for production LLM training where multi-GPU performance matters.

Missing key ablations and analysis: (1) No separate evaluation of activation filtering alone versus dimension reduction alone; (2) No analysis of which activations matter most; (3) Limited study of scaling with model depth; (4) No memory footprint analysis; (5) Unusually large batch size (one million tokens)—sensitivity unclear.

Reproducibility and generalization concerns: Code availability not mentioned; implementation complexity is high; graph stability assumption (Section 3.2.3) lacks empirical validation; special prime number markers are brittle and may collide with actual dimensions; unclear how approach extends to other frameworks (TensorFlow, JAX).

Solid empirical evaluation across three models with good ablation studies on context length and filtering ratio showing linear scaling

weaknesses: Unresolved utility-efficiency trade-off: Collider achieves 20.7 average utility vs. Rho's 24.8 (15.8% relative decrease), with the explanation that 'different hyperparameters' are needed, but without empirical validation through actual hyperparameter tuning experiments

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: Paper convincingly shows that existing token filtering achieves only 1.2% end-to-end speedup despite filtering 40% of tokens, with clear quantitative analysis of two specific barriers (inadequate sparsity and mismatched sparsity range)

Novel technical contributions: The insight that ∂Q, ∂K, ∂V have different sparsity properties and require separate processing is elegant and non-obvious. The solution is compatible with industry-standard implementations like FlashAttention

Strong empirical results in tested domains: Achieves 40-49.9% backward speedup and 17.9-34.7% end-to-end speedup when filtering 50% tokens, with consistent improvements across multiple model scales (1.1B-40B) and training scenarios (DP, TP, LoRA)
Practical implementation with minimal integration overhead: Requires only 1-5 lines of code changes to existing systems, with open-sourced codebase and automatic graph updating workflow
Comprehensive system design: Thoroughly addresses the challenge of dynamic computation graphs in PyTorch through automatic code generation, special markers, and a two-phase offline/online approach
Clear presentation and extensive documentation: Well-written paper with clear figures, logical flow, and detailed appendices explaining implementation decisions
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope undermines generalizability claims: All 9 evaluation tasks are math-focused (GSM8K, MATH, SVAMP, etc.) with no evaluation on general language modeling, translation, QA on other domains. Claims about 'unlocking full efficiency in LLM training' are overstated

Only fine-tuning experiments, no pre-training validation: All experiments fine-tune pre-trained models; no evaluation on pre-training from scratch, which is the primary scenario where training efficiency matters most at scale

Evaluated on relatively small models only: Maximum 40B parameters tested, while modern LLM training involves 70B+, 100B+, models where efficiency gains are most critical. Scalability of overhead beyond 40B is unaddressed

Graph transformation overhead scaling is concerning: Filter operator overhead increases from 2.98s (1.1B model) to 14.54s (40B model); no analysis of how this scales to 100B+ models, raising questions about practical utility at production scale

Runtime stability assumption lacks formal validation: Entire system design depends on computation graph remaining stable during training, an implicit assumption that could fail with dynamic batching, different attention implementations, or conditional computation—not formally proven or thoroughly tested

Fragile graph updating implementation: Relies on code generation, special markers (prime numbers), and greedy algorithms to identify dimensions; this pragmatic approach is vulnerable to PyTorch version changes, different model implementations, and edge cases not explicitly handled

Incomplete analysis of baseline failures: Strawman approach fails to converge (Figure 4) but mechanistic explanation for why is unclear. Why separate processing in CENTRIFUGE avoids the interference issue needs deeper analysis

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against standard training and naive token filtering; no comparison with other sparse computation frameworks, structured pruning, quantization, or alternative efficiency techniques that might achieve similar gains

Utility improvements are not from CENTRIFUGE: Table 1 shows 9.5-26.6% utility improvements come from the underlying token filtering method, not CENTRIFUGE itself, which only preserves these gains. CENTRIFUGE's actual contribution to model quality is neutral

PyTorch-centric design limits portability: Solution tightly coupled to PyTorch's dynamic graphs and implementation details; unclear how it would transfer to TensorFlow, JAX, or other frameworks where different graph structures may require extensive redesign
